finding: The live range of $290-$1,400 is about right: the floor matches what we can build, and the ceiling is higher than our own totals but lower than what two of the outside estimators show, so there is no evidence to narrow it. Our totals, built as radiator price plus stated hours at $120-$160 per hour (a national middle rate), radiator only with no coolant, are: economy 2015 Corolla 1.8L $275-$711; midsize 2016 Honda Pilot $343-$1,016; truck 2016 F-150 5.0L $260-$506 (about $797 with the dearer of the two Ford radiators listed for that engine, $637.07 list); luxury 2016 Acura MDX $547-$1,016. So the built span is about $260-$1,016. The cheapest cases, an aftermarket radiator on a Corolla or F-150, land within $30 of the live floor. Nothing we built reaches $1,400, but our numbers leave out coolant, hoses and shop parts markup and lean on warranty times, and the outside estimates run higher: RepairPal $1,368-$1,550, ConsumerAffairs $750-$1,850 from mechanic quotes, J.D. Power about $700-$1,000 (2022), YourMechanic $1,043-$1,216 for a Toyota Tundra. Jerry ($236-$377) is the one low outlier and contradicts its own text. The gap with RepairPal is in parts: it assumes $993-$1,001 for the radiator, where genuine list prices we found are $346-$424 and aftermarket $71-$140; its labor ($375-$550) is in line with our 2-3.7 hour classes. A fair reading is that $290 is a real floor for a simple vehicle with an aftermarket radiator, most jobs fall between about $450 and $1,000, and quotes up to $1,400 or somewhat more happen with dealer parts pricing, hoses, coolant and thermostat added. Weak points in the labor times: none is a plain radiator-only time for the example vehicle. Economy uses a Hyundai Kona warranty time (1.7 hr, includes a leak inspection) and a Nissan LEAF campaign time (2.2 hr, combined with a condenser bolt, on an electric car) because no Corolla time was found. Midsize runs from a Hyundai Palisade warranty time (2.0 hr) to Honda's own 3.7 hr for the Pilot, which also covers hoses, an engine flush and an inspection. Luxury is the same Honda bundled 3.7 hr on the MDX with no second figure, so its low total ($547) is probably too high for a plain radiator swap. Truck is a seller's approximate one hour (the same seller says two hours for the previous-generation truck). The Pilot and MDX share one radiator (19010-5J6-A01), so those two classes differ only in the labor figures we could find. For context only, and not used in our numbers: Ford bulletins for the 2015-2019 Transit van give 2.8-3.7 hours (gasoline engines) for a combined job of fan clutch test, thermostat inspection, cooling system flush and radiator replacement. No Kelley Blue Book radiator figure could be found by search.
extras: A quote often adds coolant and a cooling system bleed or pressure test (not included in the parts figures here), upper and lower radiator hoses and clamps, a radiator cap, a thermostat, transmission fluid top-up on vehicles where the transmission cooler is built into the radiator, a diagnosis fee, shop supplies, coolant disposal, and sales tax. If the engine overheated before the repair, a shop may also recommend checks for further damage. The parts figures here are the radiator only.
